To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a bioinformatics workflow for whole-genome sequencing data can be validated for routine use in a national reference laboratory, with high performance for the characterization of antibiotic resistance genes, typing schemes, and serogroups of Neisseria meningitis isolates.

a WGS workflow for routine use is a valid alternative to conventional molecular typing methods and that it is feasible to validate such a workflow in a small-scale laboratory setting, with the aim of replacing classical typing methods in a public health context.

(a) we present a validation strategy that focuses specifically on the exhaustive bioinformatics characterization of a WGS pipeline designed to replace conventional methods for pathogen typing in a representative small laboratory, (b) we demonstrate high performance of our workflow with values for all evaluated performance metrics >87% and >97% for the resistance characterization, sequence typing assays, respectively, and >90% and >97%, respectively, for the serogroup determination assay for both validation datasets,
In summary, our research is concerned with
the urgent need for a harmonized framework for WGS workflows and related validation strategies for routine molecular typing in a national reference center.
the validation of a WGS-based bioinformatics workflow for routine use in a national reference center, as well as with the challenges and requirements for such validation.

the validation of the bioinformatics workflow for routine analysis of WGS data, which we have developed and implemented for the characterization of N. meningitidis isolates in a small-scale laboratory setting, and the related challenges that we have encountered during the process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the WGS workflow is “fit-for-purpose”, but only for the specific validation dataset used in this study and the specific bioinformatics analysis performed
our WGS workflow is fit-for-purpose and that the bioinformatics analysis thereof provides high-quality results.

our WGS workflow can be implemented in a small-scale laboratory setting and is fit-for-purpose for the routine molecular typing and characterization of N. meningitidis isolates, as well as for the identification of resistance genes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we developed and validated a WGS workflow that can be used for molecular typing and pathogenicity characterization of N. meningitidis and that our validation strategy can be used for other pathogens as well.
we have developed a WGS workflow for N. meningitidis, which has been validated in a small-scale laboratory and which has been made publicly accessible as a “push button” pipeline for Illumia data.
we demonstrate the feasibility of WGS as a replacement method for routine molecular typing, with the added value of providing a more comprehensive characterization of the analyzed samples.
The main takeaway from our work is that
WGS can be successfully employed for pathogen typing and pathogen-related challenges in routine molecular typing and characterization, but only if the bioinformatics analysis is thoroughly validated.

, in addition to the technical and computational challenges of WGS workflows, the validation process itself is a major bottleneck for the routine application of WGS for pathogen typing in a quality-assured environment, which requires the development of a harmonized framework for the validation of bioinformatics workflows.

WGS is indeed a “fit-for-purpose”, high-quality, and robust method for routine molecular typing, but that the required bioinformatics analysis and its validation are still challenging and require substantial resources.
